notes: Draft was right. Two versions of the surface number exist: NASA/JPL and SwRI press material say 0.67 mSv/day; the Science paper (Hassler et al. 2014) reports 0.64 +/- 0.12 mSv/day. For the cruise NASA says 1.8 mSv/day ('The RAD data showed the Curiosity rover was exposed to an average of 1.8 milliSieverts of GCR per day on its journey to Mars'); the paper reports 1.84 +/- 0.33. Guo et al. 2021 state the cruise value was later revised down about 15% to 1.58 +/- 0.22 mSv/day (Zeitlin et al. 2019 reanalysis). The two Science papers are paywalled: I read only their abstracts; the central values 0.64 and 1.84 were confirmed in an open-access paper that cites them, the +/- uncertainties come from secondary citations. Safest wording for the game: 'about 0.67 mSv a day on Mars, about 1.8 mSv a day on the way there (NASA/JPL, 2013)'. PIA17601 breaks the ~1 sievert mission into 180 days out, 500 days on the surface and 180 days back, with roughly equal contributions from the three stages.

notes: Verified, and there are real numbers for the game's trade-off. Orion: 'the crew will use stowage bags on board Orion to create a dense shelter'; the bags hold 'supplies, food and water'. Regolith: the NASA Langley papers say 'regolith offers excellent shielding properties at thicknesses of 3 to 7 m' and that 'three meters of regolith results in an approximate annual dose of 50 mSv ... Seven meters of regolith give an annual dose approximately equivalent to Earth background levels, ~5 mSv.' The regolith table is a design guideline from a NASA conference paper, for cosmic rays only, not an agency requirement; the paper warns that a full transport analysis is needed for accurate numbers. The key lesson is non-linear: 12 cm of soil 'Meets typical SPE requirement' (solar storms) but barely lowers the cosmic-ray dose (0.51 to 0.46 mSv/day); it takes about 3 m to cut it to a quarter. Water: NASA-STD-3001 states storm shielding in centimetres of water equivalent, and the Lunar Safe Haven paper says 'high hydrogen-content materials like polyethylene or water are more effective shielding materials per mass' but are less dense than regolith, while using local regolith 'greatly reduces the delivery mass to surface needed'.

Measured during the pass through the Van Allen proton belt, the fourfold gap is between the most shielded sensor (on the back of the Helga phantom) and the two least shielded ones on the cabin wall. The storm shelter itself measured about 2 times better than the cabin wall (287 versus 134 microgray/minute). The 4 times for the shelter comes from a simulation of the October 1989 solar storm (414 versus 95 microgray/minute). Safe wording: 'where you sit in Orion can change your dose rate up to four times'. Helga and Zohar: NASA says 'Zohar will wear a radiation protection vest, called AstroRad, while Helga will not'. Artemis II: flew. Launch at 6:35 p.m. (Eastern time) on 1 April 2026 from Launch Pad 39B at Kennedy Space Center; splashdown 5:07 p.m. PDT on 10 April 2026 off San Diego; crew Reid Wiseman (commander), Victor Glover (pilot), Christina Koch and CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen (mission specialists); Orion was named Integrity. Radiation facts published by NASA before the flight: six HERA sensors, a Crew Active Dosimeter in each astronaut's pocket (first use beyond Earth orbit) and DLR's M-42 EXT sensor. UNVERIFIED: the dose the Artemis II crew actually received - I found no NASA figure; a '12 mSv' number on a non-NASA site could not be confirmed. The 6.97-7.61 mGy value is a 2023 pre-flight projection, not a measurement.

claim: The Sun's activity rises and falls in a cycle of roughly 11 years; on 15 October 2024 NASA, NOAA and the Solar Cycle Prediction Panel announced that the Sun had reached the solar maximum period of Solar Cycle 25; galactic cosmic rays get in more easily at solar minimum.

Peak monthly smoothed sunspot number of Solar Cycle 25, reached in October 2024 (SILSO, Royal Observatory of Belgium)
Cosmic rays striking a golf-ball-sized volume of space each second ('some')

source_title: NASA, NOAA: Sun Reaches Maximum Phase in 11-Year Solar Cycle (NASA, Oct. 15, 2024)
quote: representatives from NASA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and the international Solar Cycle Prediction Panel announced that the Sun has reached its solar maximum period, which could continue for the next year.

extra_sources.title: How NASA Will Protect Astronauts From Space Radiation at the Moon (NASA, Aug. 7, 2019) - cosmic rays and the solar cycle
STCE / SILSO: Solar Cycle 25 reached its maximum in October 2024

notes: Draft was right. Cycle length: 'Roughly every 11 years, at the height of the solar cycle, the Sun's magnetic poles flip'. NASA quote for cosmic rays (2019 article): 'In the relative calm of solar minimum, cosmic rays easily infiltrate the Sun's magnetic field. But during solar maximum, the Sun's magnetic bubble strengthens with increased solar activity, turning away some of the galactic visitors who come knocking.' The October 2024 announcement was about the maximum PERIOD, not the peak month; NOAA's Elsayed Talaat said the peak month 'will not be identified for months or years'. Later, the Belgian sunspot data centre SILSO reported that the smoothed sunspot number peaked in October 2024 at 161 (not a NASA or NOAA statement). Trade-off for the game: solar maximum means more solar storms but fewer cosmic rays; solar minimum is the reverse.

notes: All draft items check out, and one event was missing: the X8.1 flare of 1 February 2026 (6:57 p.m. ET; 23:57 UTC), now the third strongest of the cycle. Exact NOAA wording for the radiation storm: the storm 'has intensified to Severe (S4) on the NOAA Space Weather Scales' and 'This significant level has not been observed since October, 2003.' Exact NASA wording for May 2024: 'a rating of G5 — the highest level on the geomagnetic storm scale, and one that hasn't been seen since 2003.' The X5.1 flare was followed by a G4 WATCH and the G4 level was actually reached at 01:20 UTC on 12 Nov 2025; NASA's DONKI lists a maximum Kp of 8.67 for both the 12 Nov 2025 and the 19 Jan 2026 storms, so neither reached G5. 'X9.0 is still the strongest of the cycle' was checked on 11 November 2026 against the SpaceWeatherLive ranking, which is not a NASA or NOAA page. The 20 May 2024 X12 flare in R3 is an estimate from Solar Orbiter data, not an Earth-side GOES measurement (DONKI lists no X-class flare on that date), so it is not in these lists. Flare times are UTC; the X9.0 peaked at 8:18 a.m. Eastern time.

claim: Without countermeasures, astronauts' weight-bearing bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of their mineral density per month in space; ISS crews exercise about two hours a day; and NASA's Twins Study (Scott Kelly, 340 days in space, compared with his twin Mark on Earth) found that most changes returned to normal after landing.

notes: Draft was right. A second NASA page words the bone figure as 'roughly 1% less dense' for every month in space 'if they don't take precautions'. Twins Study headline findings, in NASA's words: gene expression - 'Most of these changes (about 91.3%) reverted to baseline after he returned to Earth; however, a small subset persisted after six months'; telomeres - 'Scott experienced a change in telomere length dynamics during spaceflight and within days of landing'; immune system - Scott got a flu vaccine in space and 'Scott's body reacted appropriately to the vaccine'; thinking - 'Scott's cognitive performance ... remained largely unchanged during his time in space'; blood vessels - 'indications of inflammation and carotid artery wall thickening'; gut bacteria - 'profoundly different during flight from preflight'. NASA's summary also lists what stayed changed at the end of the study: 'a small subset of changes in gene expression, telomere dynamics, DNA disruption, carotid artery thickening, ocular changes, and some cognitive functions'. It is a study of one pair of twins, so present the findings as examples rather than general rules (my caution, not a NASA quote).

claim: NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) is NASA's free, open archive of space-biology data - omics, physiological, behavioural and environmental-telemetry data from spaceflight and ground experiments on humans, animals, plants and microbes.

datasets.category: a - plants grown on the ISS (Veggie)
datasets.title: Microbiological and nutritional analysis of lettuce crops grown on the International Space Station-VEG01A
datasets.finding: Red romaine lettuce ('Outredgeous') grown in the Veggie chamber on the ISS tested negative for the screened human pathogens; the study concluded leafy crops can provide safe, edible fresh food for astronauts.

datasets.category: a - plants grown on the ISS (Veggie)
datasets.title: Stress and light spectral quality influence the transcriptome of a tomato crop on the International Space Station
datasets.finding: Tomato ('Red Robin') grown in Veggie (VEG-05, 2022-2023) under red-rich or blue-rich light showed gene-activity changes caused by both spaceflight and the light colour.

datasets.category: a - plants in Moon soil (ground study, bonus for a Moon outpost)
datasets.title: Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith present stress-associated transcriptomes that inform prospects for lunar exploration
datasets.finding: Arabidopsis plants germinated and grew in real Apollo 11, 12 and 17 Moon soil, but developed slowly and showed stress - lunar regolith can grow plants but is 'not benign'.

datasets.title: Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Exposure Activates Dose-Dependent DNA Repair Response and Downregulates Glucosinolate Pathway in Arabidopsis Seedlings
datasets.finding: Seedlings exposed to simulated galactic cosmic rays (40 or 80 cGy at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory) showed dose-dependent changes in gene activity, with DNA-repair pathways switched on.

datasets.category: b - space radiation dosimetry (OSDR tool, no OSD number)
datasets.title: Environmental Data App - ISS cabin telemetry and radiation data for spaceflight missions
datasets.finding: Shows the radiation doses (galactic cosmic rays, South Atlantic Anomaly, total accumulated) together with temperature, humidity and CO2 recorded on the ISS during Rodent Research, APEX and VEG-01C missions.

datasets.title: Lunar gravity prevents skeletal muscle atrophy but not myofiber type shift in mice
datasets.finding: In mice housed in an artificial-gravity system on the ISS, Moon gravity (1/6 g) prevented the soleus (calf) muscle wasting seen in microgravity, but not the change in muscle-fibre type.

datasets.category: c - rodent bone and muscle loss
datasets.title: Targeting myostatin/activin A protects against skeletal muscle and bone loss during spaceflight [plasma proteomics]
datasets.finding: Normal mice lost significant muscle and bone mass during 33 days in microgravity (Rodent Research-19); blocking the myostatin/activin A signal increased muscle and bone mass.

datasets.title: Specific Host Metabolite and Gut Microbiome Alterations Are Associated with Bone-loss During Spaceflight
datasets.finding: In Rodent Research-5 mice, changes in gut bacteria and blood metabolites went together with the loss of bone mineral density seen in flight.

datasets.title: Whole Blood Measurements from the SpaceX Inspiration4 Mission (RNA-seq, epitranscriptome, WGS, clonal hematopoiesis, CBC)
datasets.finding: Blood samples from the four private astronauts of the 3-day Inspiration4 flight (16-18 September 2021), taken before and after flight; the linked paper reports spaceflight-associated increases in the RNA mark m6A.

notes: The nine OSD-numbered entries were confirmed through the OSDR API on 11 November 2026: titles are copied from the 'Study Title' field and each finding is a plain-English summary of the study description stored in OSDR (the Environmental Data App entry was read from its own page). The study pages are JavaScript apps, so a simple fetch returns an empty shell; use the metadata API (https://osdr.nasa.gov/osdr/data/osd/meta/<number>) to read them in code. Sister datasets: OSD-268 (VEG-01B) and OSD-269 (VEG-03A) for lettuce; OSD-572 and OSD-573 (microbial swabs), OSD-571 (plasma) and OSD-630 (stool) for Inspiration4; OSD-210 (seeds flown on an Antarctic balloon to sample cosmic-ray damage); OSD-581 (ryegrass on Mars soil simulant). OSDR has no OSD-numbered 'dosimetry' dataset that I could find: radiation dose data sit in two OSDR tools, the Environmental Data App (listed above) and the RadLab portal (https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/), which returned HTTP 500 when I tried it, so its content is unverified.

notes: Yes, there is a requested acknowledgement. CCMC Publications Policy: if results from CCMC tools/systems '(e.g., DONKI, Scoreboards, Kamodo, etc.) are used in a scientific publication or presentation', CCMC requests an acknowledgement, with this sample text: "We acknowledge the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) at Goddard Space Flight Center for the use of the [SOFTWARE TOOL/SYSTEM NAME], [URL OF THE TOOL ON THE CCMC WEBSITE]." The DONKI page adds 'Rules-of-the-Road': 'CCMC requests that event and validation studies with data from DONKI be performed with the knowledge and collaboration of the submitting forecasters/researchers, model developers, and CCMC', and a caution that the data 'should be considered only as prototyping quality and in research context'. Who runs it: the page says 'The Moon to Mars Space Weather Analysis Office (2020-present), CCMC (2010-2020) and other entities provide data to DONKI as a courtesy to the community.' Important for the game code: on 30 September 2026 DONKI moved to new addresses. The page says 'Replacing kauai.ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov with ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov in existing links will route directly without modification.' On 11 November 2026 the new address answered correctly, the old kauai address did not connect, and https://api.nasa.gov/DONKI/FLR with DEMO_KEY returned HTTP 404 once and then a rate-limit error, so test the api.nasa.gov route before relying on it. A suggested credit line for the game, filled in from CCMC's template: 'We acknowledge the Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) at Goddard Space Flight Center for the use of DONKI, https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI/.'
